taxonomic_note: Accepted spelling is Salvia pentstemonoides (extra t). U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service explicitly notes that penstemonoides is a common misspelling. Preserve the Master Plant Pool source spelling for provenance but use pentstemonoides for the canonical taxon.
look_here_first: LOOK at actual ROSETTE in USFWS SSA Fig. 2.1a (linked below) for broad, thick, glossy dark-green basal blades. In the installed USFWS close-up, inspect the roughly 4-cm crimson tube with upper/lower corolla lips and green-to-purple calyx; it does NOT photograph the rosette, despite misleading media-page title. Compare cedar sage's smaller crimson blooms and often 1–3 leaflet long-petioled rosette versus scarlet sage's triangular simple leaves up stems.
project_tracker_diagnostic: perennial herb with persistent basal rosette; tall stiff flowering stalk; large red/rose-red bilabiate flowers; limestone seep/stream/canyon specialization; rare Edwards Plateau endemic

project_inclusion.range_basis: Bandera — NPSOT historical/rediscovery account documents wild populations in Bandera County. Real — NPSOT account explicitly documents a private-land wild population in Real County. Kerr — NPSOT reports rediscovery of a large wild population along the Guadalupe River in Kerr County; historical Kerr specimens are also noted. Gillespie — U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service identifies the 1845 upper Pedernales type material from Gillespie County as historical backup evidence.

best_field_traits: perennial herb with persistent basal rosette
morphology_keys.habit: Long-lived perennial with thick basal rootstock and a persistent rosette, one or several flowering stalks to about 1.5 m.
morphology_keys.leaves: Smooth thick dark-green basal rosette leaves, can be as long as 12 cm; not usually pinnately 1–3-foliolate like some cedar sage.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: Tall unbranched or sparsely branched stiff four-sided flowering stalk with big tubular red to purplish-red blooms.
morphology_keys.flower_dimensions: Corolla typically around 4 cm tubular, scarlet to reddish purple. Calyx green, becoming purple with age; flower much larger than local cedar sage in typical conditions.
morphology_keys.habitat: Typically shaded/seep-moist limestone ravines, bluffs and streamside ledges, within the Edwards Plateau; a rare, conservation-sensitive wild taxon.
morphology_keys.rare_plant_caution: Do not disclose exact locations or collect wild specimens for photographs. USFWS sources indicate at-risk, narrowly distributed native.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Salvia roemeriana: Both can be red, but Big Red Sage has a much larger basal rosette, taller flowering stalk, much larger flowers, and a moist limestone-seep/canyon niche.

teach_terms.basal_rosette: Cluster of leaves at base of plant, all attaching close to ground
teach_terms.bilabiate: Flower divided into an upper and lower lip
teach_terms.corolla: Petals as a whole, including the joined flower tube

photo_diagnostic_lesson.memory_rule: BIG RED: BIG SMOOTH ROSETTE, BIG 4-cm TUBES, WET LIMESTONE BLUFFS.

anatomy_steps.simple: The red joined petals forming a long tube; Big Red Sage roughly 4 cm flower including lips.
The red terminal lobes that divide the flower into two unequal sides; upper/lower orientation matters.
The green cup around base of corolla; it can turn purplish with age and shows pointed lobes.
Sex organs are much harder to tell apart; use the labeled USFWS Fig 2.1d, not unverified arrows on field photographs.
The low cluster of broad glossy leaves at ground level. Not in the newly installed flower photo; use USFWS Fig 2.1a for real example.
